transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (AE), Sahil Kapoor (SE), Erin Park (Prod Mktg), Alex Gomez (Enablement), Jill Tan (Sales), Marcus Liu (SE), Priya Singh (Solutions), Dana O'Neill (CSM)
---
Summary: Internal enablement session focused on sharpening messaging for Redwood's hosted vs dedicated vs private story, competitive positioning vs OpenAI/Anthropic/AWS, and live demo practice highlighting latency/cost tradeoffs, KV cache explanation, and rollout/rollback talking points. Practiced a 7-minute demo with interruption handling and objections.
Topics: Messaging framework, competitor differentiation, demo checklist, demo run-through, common objections & rebuttals, next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Alright everyone welcome, thanks for jumping on, we're gonna run the quick agenda - messaging refresh, competitor callouts, then demo practice. I'll hand it to Erin for 5 minutes on the new battlecard updates.
[00:22] Erin: Cool hey team, yeah so quick update first - we've tightened the intro to frame Redwood as the production-first inference platform, so we lead with predictable economics: latency, cost, reliability. Uh, then we layer in the three deployment modes: hosted API for quick wins, Dedicated for predictable throughput, and Private for regulated environments.
[00:41] Erin: Note - we changed the wording on "private" to "Private (VPC/on-prem)" to be explicit for compliance folks, apparently "private" alone caused question marks in last week's demo.
[00:54] Marcus: Nice. Also can we add a short line about where we sit relative to OpenAI? People ask like, why not just call OpenAI?
[01:05] Erin: Yes, we added a single-sentence competitive frame: OpenAI is great for product iteration and ensembles, but Redwood focuses on delivering predictable serving economics and operational controls for production apps - routing, KV caching, quantization recommendations, and enterprise SLAs. Also called out audit logs, KMS integrations, and canary rollouts.
[01:26] Sahil: One note - watch the phrase "predictable serving economics" in 1:1s, it can sound abstract. Try reframing as "we help reduce per-token costs while keeping latency guarantees, via caching, batching, and optimized kernels".
[01:40] Maya: Good call. Alright Sahil, you take the demo checklist and we'll run a 7-minute demo. Pretend the customer cares about latency and wants to know differences between Hosted and Dedicated. Try to get to the KV cache story.
[01:52] Sahil: Yep, start scenario. Hi - thanks for the time, quick context: customer is building a chat assistant with 4-8k prompt lengths, cares about latency for interactive UX and cost at scale.
[02:05] Sahil (demo): Opening the console now, so first thing, model catalog - we pick a 8-bit quantized open model, note the profile shows expected p95 latency at 128 tokens, and token-cost estimate per thousand. Then I switch to Dedicated example, show consistent throughput metrics.
[02:23] (slight pause, keyboard clicking)
[02:30] Jill: Quick interruption - when you say "8-bit quantized" some customers ask "does that affect quality?" How do we answer concisely?
[02:39] Sahil: Good question - short answer: in many workloads, quantization gives near-identical output quality with lower cost; we lean on evals and provide model/quantization recommendations per workload. Long answer: show the evaluation report in the console that compares quality delta across prompts.
[02:58] Priya: Note - add a line about "we'll run a quick eval on your prompt set" in the pitch. It removes the fear of degradation.
[03:08] Sahil: Agreed. Continuing - I open the dashboard, and highlight the per-route latency breakdown, token cost, and trace for one request. Then I show caching: here is an example prefix cache where repeated system prompts are cached in the KV cache and reduce tokenization/compute.
[03:26] (murmur: ahhh)
[03:30] Marcus: Transcription nit: sometimes demos stumble on "KV" - folks ask what the K and V are - recommend a one-liner: "KV cache stores key/value attention states to skip recomputing earlier tokens, so repetitive contexts are much faster".
[03:45] Sahil: I'll use: "Think of it as storing the model's previous attention so we don't recompute the same prefix".
[03:52] (keyboard click)
[04:00] Alex: Quick coaching note - when customers bring up "Hosted" vs "Dedicated" cost, map to use-case: Hosted for rapid dev/variable volume, Dedicated when you need predictable throughput, isolation, and commit pricing. Also call out burst policies and autoscaling for Dedicated.
[04:18] Sahil: Good. During the demo the customer asks about SSO and audit logs. I show the "Security" tab - we support SAML/SSO, role-based access control, audit trails, and KMS integration. Also show SOC 2 mention in compliance docs.
[04:36] Jill: Someone may ask about data residency - what's the short answer?
[04:40] Sahil: We say: "We have region controls and Private deployments that support customer-managed VPCs and on-prem for regulated workloads; we can keep data within chosen cloud regions or on-prem if needed."
[04:52] Priya: Also practice: if they ask about encryption at rest vs in-flight, say yes to both and mention KMS/HSM options for Private deployments.
[05:02] Maya: Good. Ok let's do a roleplay: Marcus will be the prospect, Sahil on demo, Maya will interrupt with tricky objection about latency vs cost. 7 min run, go.
[05:12] Marcus (prospect): We're seeing p95 of 500ms in our current system, if we move to Redwood what latency can we expect and at what cost?
[05:22] Sahil (demo): Great question, depends on model and sequence length; for a 2k token prompt we typically see p95 of X-Y ms on our hosted profiles, but Dedicated gives more consistent p95. The tradeoff is cost - Dedicated is more predictable per-hour but you pay for reserved capacity. We can show a cost-per-token estimate and compare.
[05:44] Marcus: But can you give a number? Customers want concrete numbers not abstract ranges.
[05:48] Sahil: Yeah, okay example: on a mid-sized 8-bit model at 512 tokens, hosted p95 is ~120-150ms, Dedicated under the same model/profile at steady state is often sub-100ms p95 depending on hardware; exact numbers vary, we should run a benchmark on their sample prompts.
[06:07] (crosstalk: interesting)
[06:10] Maya (objection): If their tolerance is <100ms, do we push Dedicated or do we say maybe custom infra? Also customers ask "why not OpenAI?"
[06:18] Sahil: For sub-100ms SLOs at scale you often need Dedicated with right hardware and an optimized runtime; we also have routing policies to route latency-critical requests to faster variants. On "why not OpenAI", we emphasize control and observability - OpenAI is a model endpoint but doesn't give you the same control over routing, VPC, or reserved capacity SLAs.
[06:38] Marcus: Follow up: what about hallucinations and quality regression after quantization?
[06:44] Sahil: We recommend using our eval suite - Redwood Optimize suggests quantization profiles per workload and sets up regression alerts tied to prompt sets. If a profile shows regressions, we recommend rolling back or using a higher-precision variant.
[06:59] Jill: Good to have a short line on rollouts: canary, A/B, automatic fallback.
[07:06] Sahil: Yep I demo the rollout page - canary traffic split, auto-fall back if p95 exceeds threshold.
[07:14] (pause)
[07:20] Erin: Small product note - add the phrase "transparent performance benchmarks" to the intro; customers like seeing our verified profiles.
[07:28] Sahil: Quick critique from me: during the demo I said too many TODO's like "we can do that" - instead be specific: "we will run a 1-hour benchmark with your 100 most common prompts and share results within 3 business days".
[07:44] Maya: Yeah specificity builds credibility. Also call out artifacts to send after: pricing worksheet, compliance pack, benchmark template, recording.
[07:52] Alex: Let's run a lightning practice on competitive objections. I'll throw one, you respond in 30 seconds. "Customer: 'Why not Anthropic's Claude?'"
[07:59] Sahil: Short: Claude is strong on instruction-following and safety; Redwood focuses on serving - predictable latency, cost controls, and enterprise controls. If they need Claude's model capabilities we can host comparable open models or route to third-party endpoints, but Redwood is about making inference predictable at production scale.
[08:22] Alex: Good. Next: "Customer: 'We already use AWS SageMaker endpoints'"
[08:27] Sahil: SageMaker is fine for model hosting, but Redwood adds runtime optimizations like KV caching, continuous batching, and quantization guidance out-of-the-box plus the product-level routing, rollout, and cost analytics that make it easier for engineering teams to operate inference at scale.
[08:45] (laughter)
[08:50] Maya: Ok last segment - demo hiccup handling. If the demo fails (latency spike, model error), do: 1) acknowledge, 2) show recorded benchmark/previous success, 3) offer to run a focused benchmark on their prompts, and 4) follow-up with logs and next steps.
[09:09] Priya: Add one-liner: "we also support automatic fallback to a stable variant to keep UX up during issues".
[09:18] Marcus: Minor point - sometimes folks care about tokenization and prompt truncation - should we show the token counter in the console?
[09:24] Sahil: Yes show token counter and truncation policy, and explain how we recommend system prompt folding and prefix caching.
[09:31] (typing)
[09:40] Maya: Alright we've got enough content. Quick recap of required assets: Erin updates battlecard, Sahil records and annotates demo + shares checklist, Maya invites AE cohort. Any other asks?
[09:52] Dana: Can we make a short 1-slide "how to handle pricing vs latency" cheat sheet for Sales?
[09:58] Erin: I'll add that.
[10:02] Maya: Perfect. Wrap. Thanks everyone.
